channel.title: Workflow on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Workflow on Best of AI

item.title: Ansible
item.description:
Playbooks describe the desired state of a machine, and Ansible connects over SSH to apply it. It needs no agent on targets. Roles and a large collection of modules cover most common tasks.

The core is free, and Red Hat sells a platform with a controller and support.

Puppet, Chef, and Terraform serve other needs. Ansible suits sysadmins who manage fleets of servers.

item.title: Apache Airflow
item.description:
Workflows are Python files that define tasks and dependencies. A web interface shows runs, logs, and failures. Hosted versions exist from cloud providers and Astronomer.

Airflow handles orchestration, not the data processing itself. It takes effort to run well at scale.

Prefect and Dagster are newer alternatives. Airflow suits data engineers who orchestrate batch pipelines.

item.title: ArborGold
item.description:
Arborists can build quotes from price lists, schedule crews, and send invoices from the field. Mobile apps let crews see jobs and update status. Customer history helps with repeat work and follow-ups.

It is aimed at small and mid-size companies. Features are practical rather than AI heavy.

Jobber and Housecall Pro are broader field service alternatives. ArborGold suits tree care businesses.

item.title: Dagster
item.description:
Developers define assets in Python and Dagster tracks lineage and freshness. A UI shows runs and dependencies, and tests run locally. Dagster Cloud offers a hosted service.

The open-source core is free. It differs from Airflow in structure, so teams moving over need to adjust.

Airflow and Prefect are alternatives. Dagster suits data engineers who want asset-based pipelines.

item.title: Floranext
item.description:
Designers take phone and web orders, print tickets, and schedule deliveries. Customer records track occasions for reminders. Online stores are built into the system.

It is a subscription product for flower shops.

Lightspeed and Shopify can work with extra setup. Floranext suits floral designers who run a shop.

item.title: Fresha
item.description:
Salons manage calendars, take payments, and send reminders. Clients find and book services on a marketplace. Reports track sales and staff performance.

The software is free to start, with fees on payments and some features.

Vagaro and StyleSeat are alternatives. Fresha suits cosmetologists and salon owners.

item.title: MassageBook
item.description:
Clients book and fill out intake forms online. Therapists record notes after each session and send reminders. A free plan covers basics, and paid plans add marketing tools.

It is built for solo practitioners and small clinics.

Vagaro and Jane are alternatives. MassageBook suits massage therapists.

item.title: Mindbody
item.description:
Studios set up classes, accept bookings, and manage memberships. Clients book through a branded app or the Mindbody marketplace. Reporting and marketing tools support growth, and AI features help with messaging.

It is a subscription product with tiered pricing.

Vagaro and Zen Planner are alternatives. Mindbody suits yoga instructors who run a studio.

item.title: MoeGo
item.description:
Groomers see appointments by staff and van, store pet profiles, and send reminders. Customers book online and pay by card. AI answers calls and messages in some plans.

It is a subscription product.

Gingr and Pawfinity are alternatives. MoeGo suits pet groomers and small pet service shops.

item.title: Passare
item.description:
Directors build arrangements, collect e-signatures, and share planning details with families. Obituary and tribute tools help families write remembrances. Reports track revenue and pre-need contracts.

It is a subscription product for funeral homes.

FrontRunner and Osiris are alternatives. Passare suits funeral directors.

item.title: Shopmonkey
item.description:
Technicians and service advisors build estimates from labor guides and parts catalogs, send them to customers for approval, and track the job through completion. Digital vehicle inspections with photos help explain recommended work. Text messaging keeps customers informed.

Shops use it to replace paper tickets and spreadsheets. Parts ordering and accounting integrations vary by plan.

Tekmetric and Shop-Ware are close alternatives. Shopmonkey suits independent repair shops.

item.title: Tekmetric
item.description:
Service advisors write estimates, send digital inspections with photos, and collect approval and payment by text or email. Reports show car count, average repair order, and technician productivity. Integrations connect to parts suppliers and accounting software.

Shops use the data to see what is working and where jobs stall. It is a subscription product with per-shop pricing.

Shopmonkey and Shop-Ware are alternatives. Tekmetric suits independent shop owners and managers.

item.title: Zen Planner
item.description:
Owners set up class schedules and membership plans, and members check in with an app or kiosk. Automated billing reduces missed payments. Reports show attendance and retention.

It is a subscription product.

Mindbody and Kicksite are alternatives. Zen Planner suits martial arts instructors who run a school.

item.title: Bardeen
item.description:
Bardeen automates repetitive work that happens on web pages. A user installs the extension, then runs playbooks that click through sites, extract data, and send it elsewhere. Typical uses include scraping lists of people from LinkedIn into Google Sheets, saving a company’s details to a CRM, or sending a meeting summary to Slack.

A natural language builder lets users describe what they want, and the AI assembles the steps, which can be edited. Triggers run automations on a schedule or when something happens, and integrations cover hundreds of apps. Sales and recruiting teams, who spend time moving data between tabs, are heavy users.

item.title: Baserow
item.description:
Baserow gives teams an easy way to build databases. It looks like a spreadsheet, but tables can link to each other, store different field types, and show data as a grid, gallery, kanban board, calendar, or form. People without coding skills build trackers, inventories, and small internal tools with it.

It is open source, so companies can run it on their own servers, which appeals to those with data residency or privacy needs. The platform has a REST API and webhooks, an application builder for interfaces, and automations that run on triggers. An AI assistant can create tables from a prompt, and AI fields can generate or classify values for each row.

item.title: Boomi
item.description:
Boomi was one of the first cloud integration platforms. Its visual builder lets teams connect applications and move data between them, with a large catalog of connectors, API management, data integration, and workflow automation in one platform. Companies use it to sync records between sales, finance, HR, and operations systems without extensive custom code.

The company has leaned into AI agents. Boomi lets teams build agents that use connected systems as tools, and offers an agent catalog and controls to track what agents are allowed to do, which matters as companies deploy many of them. Data management and master data tools help keep records consistent across systems.

item.title: Claude Cowork
item.description: Cowork takes the agent approach behind Claude Code and puts it in an ordinary app window. Instead of typing commands, you describe a job such as sorting a folder of receipts, turning notes into a report, or building a spreadsheet from several PDFs. Claude breaks the request into steps, makes a plan, works on the files you have shared with it, and reports back when it finishes. Files it reads or creates appear in a panel so you can open them.

item.title: Dropbox Sign
item.description:
Dropbox Sign lets people sign documents without printing them. You upload a file, mark where each signer needs to sign or fill in fields, and send it by email. Signers open it on any device, sign, and the finished copy is stored with an audit trail that shows who signed and when. Templates make repeat documents such as contracts and NDAs quick to send.

The product started as HelloSign and was acquired by Dropbox, which renamed it. It connects with Dropbox storage, Google Drive, Gmail, Microsoft tools, and CRM systems, so documents can be sent from where they already live. A developer API lets software companies embed signing flows inside their own products, and Dropbox has added AI features in its wider document tools.

item.title: HoneyBook
item.description:
HoneyBook is designed for people who sell services, such as photographers, designers, coaches, and consultants. A client inquiry arrives through a form, the owner sends a proposal with a contract and an invoice, and the client signs and pays online, all within a single flow. This replaces a patchwork of documents, email threads, and payment apps.

Other features support day-to-day work. Automations send reminders and follow-ups, a scheduler lets clients book meetings, and a client portal keeps messages, files, and payments in one timeline. Templates for proposals and questionnaires make repeat work faster, and AI helps draft emails and project descriptions. Reports show income and pipeline.

item.title: Housecall Pro
item.description:
Housecall Pro helps small service companies run their operations. Office staff schedule jobs and dispatch technicians on a calendar and map, customers receive confirmations and arrival notifications, and technicians use a mobile app to see their jobs, send estimates, collect signatures, and take payments on site. Invoices and payments flow into accounting.

The platform includes marketing and sales tools. Review requests, email campaigns, and a customer database help a business grow repeat work, and a booking widget lets homeowners schedule online. Some AI features answer calls and messages, help with scheduling and follow-ups, and summarize job details so owners can stay on top of the business.

item.title: Microsoft 365 Copilot
item.description: Microsoft 365 Copilot is the business version of Microsoft’s AI, and its main advantage is context. It can see your files, emails, calendar, chats, and meetings through Microsoft Graph, within the permissions you already have. In Word it drafts and rewrites documents based on other files, in Outlook it summarizes long threads and drafts replies, and in Teams it recaps meetings, lists decisions, and answers questions about what was discussed. PowerPoint can build a deck from a document, and Excel can explain formulas and analyze data with plain-language prompts.

item.title: MURAL
item.description:
MURAL gives distributed teams a shared canvas. Participants add sticky notes, diagrams, images, and text to a large board at the same time, and facilitators run sessions with tools such as timers, private mode for individual thinking, voting, and guided agendas. A big library of templates covers retros, roadmaps, design sprints, and strategy exercises.

AI assists with the messy part of workshops, which is making sense of dozens of notes. It can group sticky notes by theme, summarize a board, and generate ideas to get a session started. Integrations with Microsoft Teams, Zoom, Jira, and Slack connect boards to the tools where work gets done.

item.title: NocoDB
item.description:
NocoDB turns a database into something that feels like Airtable. Connect it to an existing SQL database or create a new one, and users see tables as spreadsheets they can filter, sort, and edit, with views as kanban boards, galleries, calendars, and forms. Non-technical colleagues get access to data without learning SQL.

It generates REST and GraphQL APIs for tables, supports permissions and webhooks, and offers automation and an AI assistant to help with fields and queries. Because it is open source, teams can host it themselves and keep data on their own servers.

item.title: SAP Signavio
item.description:
Signavio helps companies understand how their processes really work. Teams model processes in a visual notation so everyone can see the intended steps, owners, and rules, and store them in a shared repository. This makes it easier to document, improve, and standardize work across departments.

Process mining adds evidence. By reading event logs from systems like SAP ERP, it reconstructs what happened in practice, revealing delays, rework, and variants that differ from the designed flow. Analysts can then quantify the impact and decide what to fix. Collaboration and journey modeling tools help teams plan transformations such as moving to a new ERP.

item.title: Teachable
item.description:
Teachable is a platform for people who want to sell what they know. A creator uploads video lessons, text, and quizzes, organizes them into a course, sets a price, and publishes it on a branded school site. Students enroll, pay, and track their progress, and the creator gets sales and engagement data.

The platform handles the business side. It processes payments in many currencies, supports subscriptions, bundles, and coupons, and offers tools for affiliate programs and email marketing. Coaching products and downloadable files can be sold alongside courses, and certificates reward completion. AI features help draft course outlines and descriptions.

item.title: Thinkific
item.description:
Thinkific is an online course platform. Creators build courses from video, audio, text, and quizzes, organize them into chapters, and host them on a site with their own branding and domain. Students log in to learn, and the platform tracks completion and issues certificates.

Features extend beyond courses. Memberships and communities keep learners engaged, bundles and subscriptions provide pricing options, and integrations connect with email tools, payment processors, and Zapier. Businesses also use Thinkific to train customers, partners, and employees, and AI tools help generate course outlines and quiz questions.

item.title: gstack
item.description:
This repository bundles the following skills:

  • office-hours: Asks pointed questions about a product idea before any code is written.
  • plan-ceo-review: Reviews project scope and reframes the underlying problem.
  • plan-eng-review: Reviews architecture, data flow, and test plans.
  • review: Runs a production-focused code review and applies fixes automatically.
  • qa: Tests the app in a live browser and generates regression tests.
  • ship: Opens a pull request and sets up a test framework if one is missing.
  • design-consultation: Generates a full design system for the project.
  • design-shotgun: Produces several visual mockups to explore design directions.
  • cso: Runs a security audit based on OWASP and STRIDE.
  • document-release: Updates project documentation automatically.

item.title: UnleashX
item.description:
UnleashX provides voice and workflow automation. Teams configure AI agents that handle phone conversations and carry out actions across systems, such as calling leads, qualifying them, updating records, and sending follow-ups. Rules define what the worker may do.

The platform presents these as digital employees for roles like sales development and support. Outbound calling needs consent and compliance with telemarketing rules, and AI voice agents should disclose themselves.

UnleashX is paid, and independent information is limited, so run a pilot first. Alternatives include Bland AI, Retell AI, Vapi, Synthflow, and 11x. UnleashX suits small teams automating calls and follow-ups.

item.title: Celonis
item.description:
Celonis is the best-known process mining platform. Every action in business systems, such as creating an order or approving an invoice, leaves a record with a time stamp. Celonis reads these logs and rebuilds the real process, showing the paths that cases take, where they wait, and how often they deviate from the intended flow.

With that picture, teams find delays, rework, and costly exceptions. The platform quantifies the impact, suggests improvements, and can trigger automated actions or alerts. AI features answer questions about process data and recommend where to focus. Common uses include order-to-cash, procure-to-pay, and supply chain work.

item.title: Jobber
item.description:
Jobber is built for small service companies such as lawn care, cleaning, plumbing, and locksmith businesses. Owners send quotes, schedule jobs on a calendar, dispatch crews, and invoice customers, with a mobile app for the crew to see their route, take notes, and collect payment on site.

Client-facing features help win and keep work. Customers can request services online, approve quotes, pay invoices, and receive reminders and arrival notices, and a client hub keeps their history together. Automations send follow-ups and review requests. An AI assistant drafts messages and helps convert rough notes into a clear quote.

item.title: Kajabi
item.description:
Kajabi is an all-in-one platform for knowledge businesses. A creator builds a site, sells courses, memberships, coaching, and digital downloads, collects payments, runs email campaigns, and hosts a community, all from one dashboard instead of stitching together several tools.

Marketing and automation are built in. Landing pages, funnels, email sequences, and a pipeline for leads let creators sell without extra software. The AI assistant helps write copy, plan courses, and generate emails, and analytics show revenue and engagement. Mobile apps for members are available.

item.title: Noterro
item.description:
Noterro is built for small bodywork and rehab practices. Clients book online and fill in intake forms before arriving, and therapists record sessions with notes. An AI feature turns a few prompts into a structured SOAP note, saving time at the end of each appointment.

Other tools cover everyday needs: scheduling, reminders, payments, packages and memberships, and insurance claims where relevant. Reports track revenue and client retention.

Noterro is paid, with plans per practitioner. It is aimed at solo practitioners and small clinics. Alternatives include Jane, Cliniko, MassageBook, Vagaro, and SimplePractice. Noterro suits manual therapists who want simpler admin.

item.title: SimplePractice
item.description:
SimplePractice is widely used by solo and small group private practices. Clients book appointments online, complete intake forms in a portal, and join video sessions, while clinicians keep notes, treatment plans, and billing in the same system. Insurance claims can be submitted electronically.

AI features help clinicians write progress notes from session details and speed up documentation, which is a chief burden for therapists. The platform offers reminders, reporting, and a client app for messaging and payments.

item.title: StyleSeat
item.description:
StyleSeat serves independent beauty professionals. Clients search for stylists, browse portfolios and reviews, and book appointments, while professionals manage their calendar, take deposits, and process payments through the platform.

The marketplace helps new clients find providers, and the business tools handle reminders, no-show protection, and client records. Recommendations use location and preference data to match clients.

StyleSeat has a subscription for professionals and fees on some transactions. Fees for marketplace clients can be a concern for stylists with an existing following. Alternatives include Vagaro, Fresha, Booksy, Square Appointments, and Glossgenius. StyleSeat suits independent stylists and barbers.

item.title: Vagaro
item.description:
Vagaro runs the front desk for beauty and wellness businesses. Clients book online or through a marketplace app, staff manage calendars, take payments, and track inventory. Reminders and no-show protection reduce lost appointments.

Marketing tools include email and text campaigns, loyalty programs, and a presence on the Vagaro marketplace. AI answers calls and messages, helps book appointments, and suggests promotions.

Vagaro charges a monthly fee per business, with add-ons and payment processing fees. Alternatives include Fresha, Booksy, StyleSeat, Square Appointments, and Mindbody. Vagaro suits salons, spas, and studios.

item.title: Ando
item.description:
Ando rethinks team chat for a workplace where software agents work next to people. In most chat tools, AI is an add-on bot. In Ando, agents have identities, inboxes, and permissions, and they can join channels, read ongoing conversations, and message teammates, just like human members.

The product has the familiar parts of a messaging platform, including channels, direct messages, group conversations, and calls. The difference is how agents are treated: a person can assign work to an agent in a thread, and the agent can respond, ask questions, and report back. Teams can bring agents built on different models.

item.title: Claude Docs
item.description:
Claude Docs brings document writing into the chat. Instead of copying an answer from a conversation into another app, you ask Claude to draft a report, memo, or plan, and it appears as a document you can edit beside the conversation. You can revise it by typing changes directly or by asking Claude to rework sections.

Documents are stored in the Artifacts tab, so they are easy to find later and update across sessions. When the draft is ready, it can be exported to common formats such as Word, PDF, Google Docs, or Markdown. The tool handles headings, lists, and tables, and it works with files and context shared in the conversation.

item.title: Born to Found
item.description:
Born to Found guides first-time founders through the early journey. It divides company building into stages, such as validating an idea, building a first product, and finding customers, and supplies playbooks and checklists for each, so a founder knows what to focus on at their point.

An AI coach answers questions and reviews work, drawing on the founder’s stage and project details. This offers a low-cost alternative to mentors for people who lack access to experienced advisors, and a structure to keep going when the path is unclear.

item.title: AIPRM
item.description:
AIPRM saves people from writing prompts from scratch. Its browser extension adds a prompt library to the ChatGPT interface, organized by topic such as SEO, sales, customer support, productivity, and writing. You pick a prompt template, fill in details like your topic or audience, and it sends a detailed, well-structured instruction to the AI. Users can also create, save, and share their own prompts.

The library grew from community contributions, which means quality varies, though ratings and usage counts help identify useful ones. Paid plans add private prompts, team sharing, and prompt management for organizations, plus integrations with other AI tools. It is popular with marketers and SEO professionals who run the same kinds of tasks repeatedly, such as keyword clustering or content briefs.

item.title: C3.ai
item.description:
C3.ai builds packaged AI applications and a platform for developing them. Instead of starting from scratch, a company can adopt an application for a defined problem, such as predicting when equipment will fail, detecting fraud, or optimizing inventory, and connect it to their data. The platform provides tools for data integration, modeling, and deployment.

The company has moved to add generative AI. Its offerings include tools that let users ask questions about enterprise data in natural language and agent features for business workflows. Customers include utilities, manufacturers, banks, and defense and government agencies, where large-scale deployments are common.

item.title: Bonsai
item.description:
Bonsai bundles the paperwork of independent work. A freelancer sends a proposal, converts it into a contract with e-signature, tracks time or milestones, sends an invoice, and receives payment. A client portal keeps everything in one place, which helps a one-person business look established.

Additional tools cover running the business. Expense tracking, tax estimates, and banking features support finances, and workflow automations send reminders for unpaid invoices. AI helps draft contract language and project descriptions. Templates are available for design, consulting, development, and other fields.

item.title: JITX
item.description:
JITX approaches board design as software. Instead of drawing a schematic by hand, an engineer describes circuits and requirements in code, and the system selects parts, creates connections, and generates a board layout that satisfies rules for signal integrity, power, and manufacturing. Changes can be made by editing the description and regenerating.

That makes it easier to reuse designs, check them automatically, and explore alternatives. The platform’s solvers handle routine layout tasks, so engineers concentrate on architecture. It targets hardware teams that build complex boards and want faster iteration.

item.title: ServiceTitan
item.description:
ServiceTitan is built for home service trades. Call center staff book jobs, dispatchers assign technicians, technicians use a mobile app to quote and invoice with good-better-best pricing, and the office tracks job costs, marketing, and payroll. Everything ties to one customer record.

Data and AI help companies grow. Tools score inbound calls, flag missed opportunities, recommend pricing, and predict technician performance, and agents assist with booking and follow-ups. Reporting shows revenue per technician and marketing return.

item.title: Airtable
item.description: Airtable looks like a spreadsheet but behaves like a database. Records live in tables with typed fields such as dates, attachments, checkboxes, and links to records in other tables, which allows relationships that spreadsheets cannot handle. The same data can be shown as a grid, kanban board, calendar, gallery, or timeline, and filters and groups tailor each view. It’s used for content calendars, product roadmaps, CRM, event planning, and operations.

item.title: Asana
item.description: Asana organizes work as tasks inside projects. Each task has an owner, a due date, and a place in a larger plan, and the same project can be viewed as a list, a kanban board, a timeline, or a calendar. Teams use it for campaign planning, product launches, client work, and operations requests, anywhere several people need to see who is doing what and by when. Portfolios and Goals roll individual projects up into a view managers can read without opening every one.

item.title: Bubble
item.description:
Bubble lets people build real web apps without programming. The editor works by placing elements on a page, defining a database, and setting up workflows that say what happens when a user clicks or a condition occurs. Apps can include logins, payments, and integrations with other services.

It is used for marketplaces, internal tools, SaaS products, and prototypes, and some companies run substantial businesses on it. AI features can generate a starting app or page layout from a description, and plugins extend functionality. Bubble hosts the app, so there is no server to manage.

item.title: Clickup
item.description: ClickUp tries to be a single home for everything a team does. At its center are tasks that can be shown as lists, boards, calendars, Gantt charts, or timelines, and each task can have subtasks, custom fields, dependencies, and checklists. Around that sit docs, wikis, whiteboards, forms, dashboards, goals, and built-in chat. Teams use it for software sprints, marketing calendars, client projects, and operations, and the same workspace can be shaped differently for each department.

item.title: Coda AI
item.description:
Coda reimagines the document as something that can behave like an app. A Coda doc can contain text, tables, buttons, and automations, so a team can build a project tracker, a wiki, a CRM, or a planning tool in the same document where they write. Formulas, similar to those in spreadsheets, connect data across the doc, and Packs integrate with outside services such as Slack, Jira, and Google Calendar.

AI features run through the platform. Coda AI can summarize documents, draft text, fill table columns with generated content, categorize and extract information, and answer questions about the contents of a doc. AI blocks and agents can be placed in workflows to automate tasks. The company joined Grammarly, which has taken the name Superhuman, and its tools are being combined with Grammarly’s writing assistant and the Superhuman email app.

item.title: DocuSign AI
item.description:
Docusign made electronic signatures routine. Senders upload a document, specify signers and fields, and recipients sign on any device, with an audit trail and legal validity in many countries. It’s used for sales contracts, HR paperwork, real estate, and any agreement that once needed a pen, and it integrates with Salesforce, Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, and many business systems.

The company has expanded to manage the whole agreement lifecycle. Its Intelligent Agreement Management platform includes tools to prepare and negotiate agreements, a repository that stores them, and AI that reads contracts to extract terms such as renewal dates, obligations, and parties. Its AI can summarize documents, answer questions about a contract portfolio, and flag risks, and workflow tools automate steps such as approvals and routing.

item.title: Gemini in Workspace
item.description:
Gemini in Workspace brings Google’s models into the apps people use at work. In Gmail, it drafts replies and summarizes long threads. In Docs, it writes, rewrites, and proofreads, and can pull in information from files and email. In Sheets, it helps create formulas, tables, and analysis. In Slides, it generates slides and images, and in Meet it takes notes and summarizes.

A side panel gives a chat assistant that can search across a user’s Drive, Gmail, and Calendar, and answer questions using that content. Organizations can control access, and Google states that business data is not used to train models without permission. Newer features include agents and tools such as NotebookLM for deeper source work.

item.title: HubSpot
item.description: HubSpot started as a marketing software company and grew into a full platform for managing the customer relationship from first visit to renewal. It is organized into hubs: Marketing Hub for email, forms, ads, and landing pages, Sales Hub for pipelines and sequences, Service Hub for tickets and help desk, Content Hub for websites and blogs, and Operations Hub for data syncing and automation. All of them read from the same CRM, so a marketer, a sales rep, and a support agent are looking at one record of the customer.

item.title: Make
item.description: Make, formerly called Integromat, lets you automate work between apps by drawing it. You place modules on a canvas for each app, such as Gmail, Google Sheets, Slack, or a CRM, and connect them with lines that show how data flows. You can add routers that split the flow into branches, filters that decide which items continue, iterators that handle lists, and functions that change data on the way. This visual layout makes complicated logic easier to follow than a long linear list of steps.

item.title: MarketMan
item.description:
MarketMan is back-of-house software for food service. Operators record what they buy and use, build recipes with ingredient costs, and see the cost of each dish. When prices change or usage varies, the system flags it, helping managers protect margins.

Ordering and invoicing are handled in one place. Staff place orders with suppliers, receive deliveries, and match invoices to what arrived, which catches errors and short shipments. Forecasting tools predict how much to order based on sales history, and integrations connect with point of sale and accounting systems.

item.title: Microsoft Power Automate
item.description:
Power Automate connects apps and automates repetitive work. Users build flows that trigger on events, such as an email arriving or a form submission, and perform actions in hundreds of services. It works smoothly with Teams, SharePoint, Outlook, and Dynamics.

AI features extend it. Copilot lets people describe a flow in plain language, AI Builder processes documents and forms, and agent capabilities handle more open-ended tasks. Desktop flows use robotic process automation to control applications that have no API.

item.title: Microsoft Power Automate
item.description:
Power Automate helps people automate repetitive work without code. In a visual designer, users create flows that start from a trigger, such as an email arriving or a form being submitted, and then run actions like saving attachments, updating a spreadsheet, sending approvals, or posting to Teams. It connects to hundreds of services, with deep integration with SharePoint, Outlook, Excel, and Dynamics 365, and handles scheduled and event-driven tasks.

It also covers robotic process automation. Desktop flows record and replay actions on a computer, allowing automation of legacy applications that lack APIs. AI Builder adds capabilities such as reading text from documents, classifying content, and making predictions, and Copilot can build a flow from a plain-language description. Newer features support AI agents that use flows as tools.

item.title: Miro AI
item.description:
Miro provides an infinite shared canvas where teams place sticky notes, diagrams, documents, and images, and work together live or asynchronously. It’s used for brainstorming, retrospectives, user journey maps, roadmaps, and workshops, particularly for distributed teams. A large library of templates, integrations with tools such as Jira, Slack, and Google Drive, and facilitation features like timers and voting make it versatile.

AI features speed up creation and synthesis. Users can generate diagrams, flowcharts, and mind maps from a prompt, summarize and cluster hundreds of sticky notes into themes, and turn a board into a document or a prototype. Sidekicks are AI helpers with specific roles, such as a product manager or a retrospective facilitator, that give feedback and suggestions on the board. Flows connect several AI steps for repeatable processes.

item.title: n8n
item.description: n8n lets you build automations by connecting nodes on a canvas, similar to Zapier or Make, but with more room for code. Each node is a step: a trigger like a webhook or schedule, an action in an app, or a block that transforms data with JavaScript or Python. Hundreds of integrations are included, and a generic HTTP node covers the rest. Workflows can branch, loop, and call other workflows, so it handles anything from simple notifications to elaborate data pipelines.

item.title: Nintex
item.description:
Nintex helps organizations digitize their processes. Using a visual designer, business analysts build workflows that route requests, collect approvals, update systems, and send notifications, and they create forms to start those workflows. It integrates with Microsoft 365, SharePoint, Salesforce, and many other systems, which is where its roots lie, with many customers automating processes on SharePoint.

The platform has several parts. Process mapping tools document how work actually happens, automation tools execute workflows and robotic process automation, and document generation tools produce contracts and reports from data. AI features assist with building workflows from descriptions and extracting data from documents, and analytics show where processes slow down.

item.title: PandaDoc AI
item.description:
PandaDoc helps sales teams close deals faster. Users build proposals and quotes from templates in a drag-and-drop editor, add pricing tables with live calculations, embed videos and payment links, and send them to clients, who can review and sign electronically. Tracking shows when a document is opened and viewed, so reps know when to follow up.

Automation and integration make it practical for teams. It connects with CRMs like Salesforce and HubSpot to populate documents with deal data and update records when documents are signed, offers approval workflows, content libraries, and a payment step. AI features help generate document content from a prompt, summarize contracts, suggest edits, and extract information, speeding up proposal creation.

item.title: Plasmic
item.description:
Plasmic connects visual design with real code. Developers register their React components in Plasmic, and designers and marketers can then drag those components onto a canvas, adjust styling and content, and publish pages without waiting for a code release. Alternatively, Plasmic can build entire pages and sites itself, and its output integrates with frameworks like Next.js, Gatsby, and plain React.

Features help teams collaborate. A CMS stores content, responsive design controls handle layouts across devices, and the editor includes interactions, animations, and data bindings. Teams can use it to build landing pages, marketing sites, and web apps, while developers stay in control of the underlying components. Code can be exported or used with a runtime, which reduces lock-in.

item.title: Proposify
item.description:
Proposify helps agencies and service companies create and send proposals. Teams build templates with sections, pricing tables, and brand styling, assemble a proposal quickly, and send it to clients who can review, comment, and sign electronically. Notifications show when a proposal is opened.

AI features help with writing content and suggest improvements based on what has worked in past proposals. Analytics reveal how long clients spend on each section, informing follow-ups. Integrations connect with CRMs and billing.

item.title: Qwilr
item.description:
Qwilr replaces static PDF proposals with web pages. A seller builds a proposal from blocks, such as text, images, videos, pricing tables, and acceptance sections, and sends a link. Buyers can adjust options in a pricing table, and sign online, which shortens the path to closing.

Analytics show who viewed the page, how long they spent on each section, and when they came back, which guides follow-up. Templates keep branding consistent, and integrations push data into CRMs. AI drafts content from notes and suggests improvements.

item.title: Raycast AI
item.description:
Raycast puts a command bar on your keyboard. Press a hotkey, type a few letters, and you can launch apps, search files, run calculations, manage windows, paste snippets, control music, and use hundreds of extensions that connect to tools such as GitHub, Linear, Notion, and Slack. Power users value how much it can cut mouse use and context switching.

Raycast AI adds chat and commands powered by leading language models. You can ask a question, rewrite selected text, summarize a page, translate, or run custom AI commands from any app, and switch among models from different providers. AI Extensions let the assistant act through extensions, such as creating an issue or checking a calendar, and Model Context Protocol support connects it to more tools. Chats and presets are synced across devices.

item.title: Salesforce Einstein
item.description:
Einstein brought AI to Salesforce customers well before generative AI became popular. Predictive features score leads and opportunities, forecast revenue, recommend next best actions, and flag at-risk accounts, using each company’s own CRM data. Einstein Discovery finds patterns and suggests what drives outcomes, and bots and analytics features extend the same ideas to service and marketing.

With generative AI, Einstein has expanded to write emails, summarize records and cases, and generate service replies, grounded in customer data and protected by the Einstein Trust Layer, which masks sensitive information and prevents customer data from being used to train outside models. The conversational assistant evolved into Agentforce, which builds autonomous agents on the same foundation, so Einstein now refers to a mix of older predictive features and the generative AI infrastructure.

item.title: ServiceNow
item.description:
ServiceNow began as an IT service management tool and became a general workflow platform for large organizations. Employees and customers submit requests, such as a laptop problem, a payroll question, or a customer complaint, and the platform routes, tracks, and resolves them using defined workflows. Companies use it as a system of record and action across IT operations, HR, legal, security, and customer service.

AI is central to its current strategy. Now Assist adds generative AI to summarize cases, draft replies, and help agents find answers, and AI agents can take on tasks such as triaging incidents and fulfilling requests with minimal human intervention. The company acquired Moveworks, whose employee assistant is intended to become the front door to the platform, and offers tools to govern and monitor agents across the enterprise.

item.title: Square
item.description:
Square is known for its card readers and registers. A small business accepts payments in person, online, or by invoice, tracks inventory, and manages staff and payroll from a single account. Hardware ranges from a simple reader to full countertop systems.

Additional services include appointments, loyalty programs, marketing, and small business loans based on sales. AI assistance writes item descriptions, generates insights from sales data, and answers business questions.

Square charges processing fees per transaction and sells hardware, with paid software tiers for advanced features. It has a free plan for basic use. Alternatives include Toast for restaurants, Clover, Shopify POS, Stripe Terminal, and SumUp. Square suits small retail and food businesses.

item.title: Sunsama
item.description:
Sunsama is built around the idea that planning your day deliberately reduces overwhelm. Each morning, a guided ritual walks you through gathering tasks from different sources, choosing what you can realistically do, estimating the time each will take, and placing them on your calendar. The app shows your total planned hours against the day’s available time, which discourages overcommitting.

It connects to many other tools. Tasks from project managers, issue trackers, email, and Slack can be brought into your daily view without leaving Sunsama, and calendar events appear alongside them. An end-of-day shutdown ritual lets you review what you finished and move unfinished tasks forward. AI features help with suggestions for scheduling, summaries, and organizing tasks.

item.title: Toast
item.description:
Toast serves the restaurant industry. Servers take orders on handheld devices, kitchen displays route tickets, guests pay at the table or online, and managers track sales, labor, and inventory. Online ordering, delivery integrations, and loyalty programs are part of the ecosystem.

Data and AI support operations. Sales forecasts help schedule staff, menu analytics show what sells, and assistants help write menu descriptions and answer business questions. Payroll and team management tools extend the suite.

item.title: Todoist
item.description: Todoist is a clean, fast task manager. You add tasks by typing in plain language, like “send report every Friday at 3pm,” and it turns that into a recurring due date. Tasks can be organized into projects and sections, given priorities and labels, and viewed as a list, board, or calendar. Filters let you build views such as everything due today across all projects. It syncs across phones, computers, browsers, and email clients.

item.title: Tray.io
item.description:
Tray.io builds on the idea of integration-platform-as-a-service. Teams use a visual builder to create workflows that connect SaaS applications, databases, and internal systems, with powerful logic, error handling, and the ability to write code where necessary. Hundreds of connectors and a universal connector for APIs cover common enterprise tools such as Salesforce, Workday, and Slack.

The company has moved toward AI agents. Its Merlin AI tools let teams build agents that use the connected systems as tools, so an agent can look up a customer, update a record, and send a message, with governance over what it can access. Embedded integration products let software companies offer customer-facing integrations in their own products.

item.title: UiPath
item.description:
UiPath popularized robotic process automation, in which software robots mimic what a person does on a screen. Developers build automations in a studio by recording and arranging steps such as clicking, copying data between systems, and filling forms, and run them on servers or desktops. This is valuable for companies with legacy systems that lack APIs, since bots can work through the same interfaces people use.

The platform has expanded into AI. Document understanding extracts data from invoices and forms, process mining reveals which workflows are worth automating, and agent tools let AI agents plan and carry out tasks, orchestrated alongside robots and people. The Maestro orchestration layer coordinates agents, robots, and human steps, and governance features control access and auditing.

item.title: Webflow
item.description:
Webflow sits between simple site builders and hand-coded sites. Designers work on a canvas that mirrors how the web works, setting classes, flexbox and grid layouts, and breakpoints, and the platform produces production code and hosts the result. That gives far more control than template-based builders, which is why agencies and in-house design teams like it.

The platform includes a CMS for blogs and collections, e-commerce, interactions and animations, localization, and tools for marketers to edit content without breaking the design. AI features generate sections and copy, suggest changes, and help with site structure and SEO. Developers can add custom code and use an API to connect Webflow to other services.

item.title: Workato
item.description:
Workato is an integration and automation platform. Teams build recipes that link applications such as Salesforce, Workday, and Slack, trigger actions, and move data. Business users can create simple automations while IT governs the platform.

The company has added AI across the product. Users describe a workflow in plain language and Workato builds a draft, document understanding extracts data, and agents handle tasks with enterprise controls. Governance, security, and monitoring suit regulated companies.

item.title: Zapier
item.description:
Zapier lets people automate work between apps without programming. A Zap starts with a trigger, such as a new form entry, and performs actions in other apps, like adding a row to a spreadsheet and sending a Slack message. It connects thousands of products.

AI has become part of the platform. Users describe an automation in plain language, add AI steps that summarize or classify data, and build agents that act across apps. Tables, forms, and interfaces let teams build small apps around their automations.

item.title: Zapier
item.description:
Zapier handles the plumbing between business apps. A workflow listens for an event in one tool and does something in another, with filters, paths, and delays to model real processes. Templates cover common needs in sales, marketing, and operations.

Newer capabilities include AI actions that read and write text, agents that carry out multi-step tasks, and an MCP offering that exposes Zapier actions to AI assistants. Teams can monitor runs, handle errors, and manage access centrally.

item.title: Zapier
item.description: Zapier connects the apps a business already uses and lets them pass data to each other without code. You build a Zap with a trigger, such as a new form submission, and one or more actions, such as adding a row to a spreadsheet, posting in Slack, and creating a CRM contact. It supports thousands of apps, from Gmail and Salesforce to niche tools, which is the main reason people choose it over building integrations by hand. Filters, paths, and delays let a Zap branch and wait, and a multi-step workflow can handle surprisingly complicated processes.

item.title: Zoho
item.description:
Zoho builds a wide range of business applications on its own platform. Companies can use Zoho CRM for sales, Books for accounting, Desk for support, Projects for work tracking, Mail for email, People for HR, and dozens of other apps, many of which integrate with one another. Zoho One bundles the whole suite for a single per-user price.

Zia is the AI layer. It predicts which leads are likely to convert, detects anomalies in data, drafts replies, and answers questions in natural language, and Zoho has added a generative assistant and agents that can act across apps. The company also supports the option of running models on its own infrastructure for customers who want data kept in their region.

item.title: Notion
item.description: Notion works as a set of building blocks. A team can create a company wiki, a project tracker with a board view, a product roadmap, a meeting notes database, and a documentation site, all in one workspace with permissions and comments. Databases are central: the same set of records can be viewed as a table, board, calendar, or timeline, and linked to other databases, which makes it possible to build custom systems without code.

item.title: Pory
item.description:
Pory turns spreadsheets and databases into websites. A user connects an Airtable base or Google Sheet, designs pages and layouts with a visual editor, and publishes a directory, portal, or dashboard. Logins and permissions control who sees what.

It is popular for member directories, job boards, simple CRMs, and client portals. Because the data stays in the source, updating the spreadsheet updates the site.

Pory has a free tier and paid plans. Complex logic is limited compared with full app builders. Alternatives include Softr, Glide, Stacker, Noloco, and Bubble. Pory suits non-developers building front ends on Airtable or Sheets.

item.title: Relay
item.description:
Relay.app takes the Zapier-style approach and adds two things: AI steps and humans in the loop. A workflow can trigger on an event, call an AI to summarize or draft, then pause for a teammate to approve before the next action runs. This suits tasks where full automation is risky.

Integrations connect common business tools, and a visual builder makes flows easy to design. Examples include drafting replies for review, routing leads, and preparing reports. Approvals can be done in email or Slack.

item.title: Activepieces
item.description: Activepieces is an alternative to Zapier built with openness in mind. Users build automations called flows by chaining a trigger, such as a new form entry, to actions across apps like Google Sheets, Slack, Gmail, and CRMs. The editor is friendly to non-developers, and code steps are available for custom logic. The integrations, called pieces, are open-source and community-contributed, and each can also work as a tool for AI agents.

item.title: Akiflow
item.description: Akiflow is built for people whose tasks are scattered across many apps. A task might arrive as an email, a Slack message, a Jira ticket, or an Asana item, and Akiflow collects them in a universal inbox so you can decide what to do and when. You drag tasks onto a calendar to block out time for them, which turns a long to-do list into a realistic day. Keyboard shortcuts and a command bar make it fast to use.

item.title: Choosaro
item.description:
Choosaro structures the way you decide. You list the options, such as three laptops or two job offers, then define the criteria that matter, like price, quality, or location, and assign each a weight. Scoring the options against the criteria produces a ranked result that shows which choice best fits your priorities.

The method is a weighted decision matrix, a familiar technique that makes tradeoffs explicit. Writing criteria down helps people notice what they really care about and gives teams a shared basis for discussion. AI features can suggest criteria and help fill in details.

item.title: Collate
item.description:
Collate focuses on private document work. A user opens a PDF, such as a paper, contract, or textbook, and asks questions about it or requests a summary. Because the processing runs locally on the device, the document does not need to leave the computer, which matters for sensitive files.

Typical uses include studying, reviewing research papers, and pulling key terms from long reports. Local models are smaller than cloud models, so results are good for summaries and questions about the text but may be less strong on complex reasoning, and speed depends on the hardware.

item.title: Denovo
item.description:
Denovo aims to shorten the path from idea to launched business. A user describes what they want to start, and the platform helps produce a business plan, suggests names and branding, generates a website, and walks through setup tasks such as registering the company. Putting these steps in one tool reduces the number of services a beginner must find and learn.

The target is people who have never started a company, or who want to test a side project quickly. AI-generated plans and sites provide a starting point, and users still need to validate demand with real customers and check legal requirements in their location.

item.title: Dora
item.description:
Dora targets people who want a standout site without writing code. A user describes the site or starts from a template, and the platform generates pages with 3D objects, scroll animations, and interactions, which are expensive to build by hand. A visual editor lets them adjust layout, copy, and motion.

Designers and small businesses use it for portfolios, landing pages, and marketing sites where visual impact matters. Compared with simple builders, it emphasizes motion and depth. Published sites are hosted by the platform, and exporting options vary by plan.

item.title: Komos
item.description:
Komos aims to replace fragile recorded scripts with instructions in natural language. A user describes a task, such as downloading reports from a portal or entering data across systems, and an AI agent carries it out by operating a browser, adjusting when a page changes.

That approach targets a known weakness of traditional robotic process automation, where small interface changes break bots. Enterprise teams use such tools for back-office tasks in systems that lack APIs.

item.title: leania.ai
item.description:
Leania.ai analyzes how work flows through an organization. It ingests information such as organization charts, process documentation, and meeting data, and uses AI to identify where handoffs are slow, roles overlap, or responsibilities are unclear. It then suggests changes to improve efficiency.

The audience is operations and HR leaders planning restructuring or process improvement. Outputs aim to replace guesswork with data from the company’s own materials, though recommendations still require leaders to understand context and consult the people involved.

item.title: Pipedream
item.description: Pipedream sits between no-code automation and writing everything yourself. You build workflows from triggers, such as a webhook or a new row in a sheet, and steps that either call a prebuilt action for an app or run your own code, with access to npm and PyPI packages. That mix lets developers move faster than in tools like Zapier while still handling logic that needs real programming, and it suits integrations and internal automations.

item.title: Reclaim AI
item.description:
Reclaim is a smart scheduling assistant. You tell it your priorities, tasks with deadlines, recurring habits such as lunch or exercise, and preferred meeting hours, and it places them in your calendar. When a new meeting appears, Reclaim moves flexible items around automatically, so your calendar stays workable without constant manual rescheduling.

Several features support teams. Smart one-on-ones find times that work for both participants and adjust over time, scheduling links let others book you at times that fit your priorities, and focus time blocks protect deep work. Integrations pull tasks from tools like Asana, ClickUp, Todoist, Linear, and Jira and schedule them, and analytics show how you spend time.

item.title: Serno
item.description:
Serno gives users a single place to consult multiple models. A person asks a question once and sees how different systems respond, with differences highlighted, which can reveal uncertainty or disagreement that a single answer would hide.

This approach suits research, strategy, and decisions where one model’s blind spot could mislead. Saved conversations and comparisons make it easy to revisit reasoning, and some workflows ask models to critique each other.

item.title: Slack AI
item.description:
Slack AI addresses the problem of catching up. When you return from time off or join a busy channel, it can summarize what happened, list decisions, and highlight what needs your attention. Thread summaries cut long discussions into a few lines, and daily recaps cover channels you choose, so you can stay informed without reading every message.

AI search turns Slack into a place to ask questions. Instead of hunting for keywords, you can ask something like what the timeline is for a project, and receive an answer drawn from messages, files, and connected apps, with links to the sources. Slackbot is being reshaped as an assistant that can help draft messages, find information, and take actions, and Salesforce’s Agentforce agents can work in Slack. Huddle notes summarize audio calls.

item.title: Slashspace
item.description:
Slashspace rethinks chatting with AI as a workspace instead of a single scrolling thread. Conversations live on a canvas where users branch ideas, keep multiple threads open, and combine sources, so research does not get buried in a long chat history.

The app supports several models, lets users bring in documents and web pages, and keeps context organized. Writers and analysts use it to explore a topic from different angles and compare lines of reasoning.

item.title: Wispr Flow
item.description:
Wispr Flow turns speech into polished text. A user presses a key, talks, and the cleaned-up text appears wherever the cursor is. The AI removes filler words, fixes false starts, handles punctuation, and adjusts tone to the app, so messages and documents read as if typed.

It supports many languages, custom vocabulary for names and terms, and commands for editing by voice. Writers, developers, and professionals use it to speed up emails, notes, and prompts for AI tools.

item.title: ZeroTwo
item.description:
ZeroTwo is a multi-model chat workspace. A user picks a model for each conversation or compares several, and keeps history, files, and prompts in one place. It supports web search, image generation, and document analysis.

For people who use several AI products, a combined interface can simplify life and cost. Pricing is typically a single subscription instead of many.

Access to the newest features of each provider may lag the official apps. ZeroTwo has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Poe, TypingMind, ChatHub, OpenRouter’s chat, and Open WebUI. ZeroTwo suits power users who work across models.
